Clark’s question was ﬁnally answered in 1995 by Murakami and Yasuhara [30] using the Gordon-
Litherland pairing. To do this, they ﬁrst proved the following necessary condition for a knot K to
bound a β1 = 2 nonorientable spanning surface F.
Theorem 4.1 (Murakami-Yasuhara [30]). There is a pair of curves generating H1(F;Z) such that
the Goeritz matrix of F takes the form:

and satisﬁes σ(K) = sign(GF (K)) −(l + 2m + n), where l,n are odd and m is even.
Consider, as in [30], the knot 74. This knot has 3-genus 1 and hence C(74) ≤3. Since 74 is
hyperbolic, we have C(74) ≥2. It therefore suﬃces to show that C(K) ≠2. Now, suppose that
C(K) = 2. Since 74 has determinant 15, one can write out integral binary quadratic forms with
determinant 15 (see e.g. Conway-Sloane [8]). Using a case analysis, it is then possible to show that
no such binary quadratic form satisﬁes Theorem 4.1. Hence, it follows that C(74) = 3 = 2⋅g(74)+1.
Crosscap numbers are in general diﬃcult to compute. Yet progress is currently being made. For
example, Kalfagianni-Lee [19] determined upper and lower bounds on the crosscap numbers for
several families of knots in terms of the coeﬃcients of the Jones polynomial.
4.3. Non-orientable slice genus. The (smooth) 4-genus of a knot K is the smallest genus among
all surfaces properly embedded in B4 such that ∂F = K. A well-known lower bound on the 4-genus
is ∣σ(K)∣/2. In analogy with crosscap number, the (smooth) non-orientable slice genus γ∗(K) of a
knot K in S3 is deﬁned as the smallest ﬁrst Betti number of all compact connected non-orientable
surfaces F smoothly embedded in B4 such that ∂F = K. If K is slice, then γ∗(K) is deﬁned to be
0. In 1975, Viro [39] showed that γ∗(41) = 2, and hence 41 does not bound a Möbius band in B4.
Another proof that γ∗(41) = 2 follows from a result of Yasuhara, which is proved using the
Gordon-Litherland pairing. Recall that the quadratic form q ∶H1(F;Z/2Z) →Z/2Z of a knot K
is deﬁned by q(x) = x⊺Ax, where F is a Seifert surface of K and A is a Seifert matrix for F. The
Arf invariant of K is the Arf invariant of this quadratic form. Hence, Arf(K) = 0 if q maps a
majority of elements of H1(F;Z/2Z) to 0 and otherwise Arf(K) = 1. The Arf invariant is also the
(mod 2) coeﬃcient of z2 in the Conway polynomial of K. Note that there is a well-deﬁned injection
Z/2Z →Z/8Z given by x →4 ⋅x.
